posts.title: A week in the cellar at 11 °C
posts.excerpt: Elif Arslan spends the week turning, brushing and washing the wheels under the counter, at 11 °C and 92 % humidity.
posts.content:
The cellar at Noka Cheese sits under the counter in Old Dairy Yard, Brookmere. It is held at 11 °C and 92 % humidity. That pair of figures is the climate we actually keep, and it is the climate Elif Arslan works in. She is the cellar keeper. She turns, brushes and washes the wheels. Upstairs the shop has been open since 2014, with one counter and about sixty cheeses in six styles. Noa Kessler still buys every wheel herself. Nothing is cut for the paper until it has been looked after down here.

A week in the cellar is the same day, repeated. At 07:30 Elif turns and brushes the wheels while the door upstairs is still shut. At 09:30 the counter is set and the wires are checked. At 10:00 the doors open. At 11:00 board pickups start. At 14:00 Samuel Adeyemi confirms tomorrow's reservations. At 18:00 reservations close for the next day. At 19:00 every cut face is re-wrapped and the counter is cleared. Elif's hour is the first of those lines. Tomás Reyes, Grace Owusu and Mei Chou cut and wrap later from wheels she has already turned.

Washed rinds take the most of her hands. They are cow's milk cheeses with an orange rind, washed in brine twice a week. The rind is sticky. The tool is a brush. Twice a week is the rhythm in this room, not a special wash put on for a photograph. Small wheels from Ostra Creamery, where two cheesemakers work, finish here instead of arriving already done. When a wheel is ready it goes up to the counter. We cut it with the wire, weigh it in front of you, and wrap it. The cheese of the month is one 250 g wedge of that month's washed rind, at €12. The washed-rind style on the counter is €4.90 / 100 g.

The room is not only orange rinds. Fresh and lactic cheeses, cow or goat, with no rind, were made this week and need the cool so they stay bright. Bloomy rounds of cow's milk, white rind, ripened 4–6 weeks, wait until they are soft to the edge. Alpine wheels from Vell Alpine Cooperative are raw cow's milk from summer pasture, held for 18 months, nutty and hard. Those are cut upstairs with the two-handled knife. Blue from Lowmere Sheep Dairy is the one blue they make, from October to May. We cut it from the wheel. We never put it out pre-packed. Goat cheeses from Hollin Ridge Farm, fresh and ash logs, follow kidding in spring. Henrik Dahl visits all four makers twice a year. What he and Noa agree to buy is what ends up on Elif's shelves.

The humidity is why the cellar is there. A cut face dries if it is left open, which is why so much cheese elsewhere is already dull by the time it is in a packet. Here the wheel stays whole until you ask. If a wheel is open on the counter during the day, the face is re-wrapped at 19:00. We use two-layer cheese paper. The name and the date go on the fold, with a line on how to keep it. At home that line means the paper stays on, the fridge at 4–8 °C, and the wedge out for 45 minutes before you eat. 150 g is a good wedge for two. The tasting happens upstairs, on the knife tip, but the cellar is why that sliver and the wedge you take home still belong to the same wheel.

Saturday changes the pace at the counter, not the morning below. Grace Owusu leads tastings at 10:30 and 15:00. Each one is 45 minutes, six cheeses, no more than eight people, €18 a person. The pieces on that table were kept down here during the week. Mei Chou wraps at the weekend. Samuel still confirms a reservation by email. If you want a board the next day, it has to be reserved by 18:00. Pickup is from 11:00 at the counter, Old Dairy Yard, 9 Tannery Lane. We do not ship from the cellar or from the shop. There is no carrier to meet.

Noa buys every wheel she would be happy to cut for a friend, and she would rather tell you we are out than sell you the wrong one. That is the buying rule. Elif's week is the keeping rule: turn, brush, wash, and hold the room at 11 °C and 92 %. Between those two habits the counter can stay specific. Come in, say what the cheese is for, and taste two or three slivers. We will cut with a wire or a two-handled knife, weigh the piece in front of you, and send it home with its name still written on the paper.

posts.title: Kidding season at Hollin Ridge
posts.excerpt: Goat's milk cheeses from Hollin Ridge Farm, fresh and ash logs, with kidding in spring.
posts.content:
Hollin Ridge Farm keeps the goats that make our fresh cheeses and the ash-coated logs. Henrik Dahl visits twice a year, once in spring when the kids are born and once in autumn when the herd comes down from the high pasture.

Fresh goat cheese is made the week it reaches us, which is why it is bright and lactic and why we sell it for only a few days. The ash logs are left a little longer to grow a thin grey rind and a firmer centre.

Because the milk follows the seasons, so does the counter. In winter there is less goat cheese and we say so when you ask, rather than fill the space with something else.

posts.title: Six cheeses on a Saturday
posts.excerpt: Grace Owusu's tasting: 45 minutes, six cheeses, at 10:30 and 15:00.
posts.content:
Each Saturday Grace Owusu sets a long table with six cheeses, one from each of our styles: fresh, bloomy, washed rind, alpine, blue, and goat or sheep. The tasting runs for 45 minutes and seats at most eight people.

The cheeses are tasted from the mildest to the strongest, with water and bread between them. Grace says where each one comes from and how it was cut, and guests are asked what they notice before they are told anything.

Tastings are at 10:30 and 15:00 and cost €18 per person. They are reserved in the shop the same way as a board, and Samuel Adeyemi confirms each booking by email.
